meta.title: OAuth2 Authorization Flows - S-Jiffy
meta.description: Interactive reference for OAuth 2.0 grant types and flows
desc: Interactive reference for OAuth 2.0 grant types and flows
ui.1: Suitable for devices with limited input capabilities. More complex UX but necessary.
ui.2: After the user authorizes, the device obtains an access_token
ui.3: The device polls the token endpoint to check whether the user has completed authorization
ui.4: The user visits the verification URL in a browser on another device
ui.5: The device shows the user_code and verification URL
ui.6: The authorization server returns device_code, user_code, and the verification URL
ui.7: The device requests a device code from the authorization server
ui.8: An authorization flow for browserless devices (smart TVs, CLI tools, etc.).
ui.9: Recommended for public clients. PKCE effectively prevents authorization code interception attacks.
ui.10: The client uses the token to access protected resources
ui.11: The authorization server returns an access_token
ui.12: The authorization server verifies that code_verifier matches code_challenge
ui.13: The client requests the token endpoint with the authorization code + code_verifier
ui.14: The authorization server returns the authorization code via the callback URL
ui.15: The user logs in and authorizes
ui.16: The client sends code_challenge and the redirect URL to the authorization server
ui.17: The user visits the client application
ui.18: The client generates code_verifier and code_challenge
ui.19: Improved authorization code flow for public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) that prevents authorization code interception attacks.
ui.20: Not recommended. The client handles user passwords. Migrate to the authorization code flow.
ui.21: The authorization server verifies the user's identity
ui.22: The client sends the user's credentials to the token endpoint
ui.23: The user enters their username and password in the client
ui.24: The user provides username and password directly to the client, which exchanges them for tokens.
ui.25: No user involvement; only suitable for trusted clients. Token scope is limited.
ui.26: The authorization server verifies the client's identity
ui.27: The client (server-side application) requests the token endpoint with its own client_id and client_secret
ui.28: For server-to-server communication without user authorization. The client obtains tokens directly with its own credentials.
ui.29: Not recommended. The access_token is exposed in the URL, which is less secure. Use authorization code + PKCE instead.
ui.30: The client extracts the token from the URL
ui.31: The authorization server returns the access_token via the URL fragment (#)
ui.32: The client redirects the user to the authorization server (/?response_type=token&client_id=...)
ui.33: Simplified flow that returns the access_token directly without an authorization code. Suitable for pure front-end applications.
ui.34: The most secure flow; supports refresh_token. Recommended with PKCE.
ui.35: The authorization server returns access_token (and refresh_token)
ui.36: The client requests an access token from the token endpoint using the authorization code
ui.37: The authorization server returns the authorization code to the client via the callback URL
ui.38: The client redirects the user to the authorization server (/?response_type=code&client_id=...)
ui.39: The most commonly used authorization flow, suitable for server-side applications. The client first obtains an authorization code, then exchanges it for an access token.
